title: The Teacher Who Told Me I Wasn't Stupid
script: Narrator: [honestly] For most of school, I believed I was simply not smart. Numbers confused me, and I always felt behind everyone else in class.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Teachers moved fast, and I was too embarrassed to raise my hand and ask them to explain something again.
Narrator: [reflective] In my last year of high school, a new math teacher joined our school. Her name was Ibu Ratna.
Narrator: [gently] On the first day, she said something I never forgot. She said, nobody in this room is stupid, only unprepared.
Narrator: [warmly] She stayed after class every week for students who wanted extra help, without ever making anyone feel embarrassed for asking.
Narrator: [honestly] I went to her almost every Friday, nervous each time, sure she would eventually get tired of my questions.
Narrator: [softly] She never did. She explained the same idea five different ways until something finally made sense in my head.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Slowly, my grades improved, not dramatically, but enough that I stopped dreading math tests every single week.
Narrator: [with feeling] More importantly, something changed inside me. I started believing that struggling with a subject did not mean I was incapable.
Narrator: [reflective] Years later, I went back to studying, this time for a certificate in accounting, something I never imagined possible before.
Narrator: [warmly] Whenever a lesson felt difficult, I remembered her voice, calm and patient, telling me to try one more time.
Narrator: [gently] I finished that course last year, and I sent her a message to thank her for everything she taught me.
Narrator: [with a small smile] She wrote back and said she still remembers me clearly, the quiet student who never gave up asking questions.
Narrator: [peacefully] Now, when I meet someone struggling to learn something new, I try to speak the same patient words she once gave me.
Narrator: [warmly] A good teacher does not just teach a subject. She teaches you that learning is still possible, no matter how late it starts.
Narrator: [gently] I think about her often, especially when a new challenge at work makes me feel small and unprepared again.

quiz.question: What did the narrator believe about herself for most of school?
options: That she was the smartest student
That she was simply not smart
That she hated her teachers
That school was too easy
quiz.explanation: She says she believed she was simply not smart, and numbers always confused her.

quiz.question: What did Ibu Ratna say on her first day teaching?
options: Everyone must study alone
Nobody in this room is stupid, only unprepared
Math is too hard for most people
Only fast students will pass
quiz.explanation: She told the class that nobody was stupid, only unprepared.

quiz.question: What did the teacher do every week for students who needed help?
options: She ignored their questions
She stayed after class for extra help
She gave them extra homework only
She sent them to another teacher
quiz.explanation: She stayed after class every week for students who wanted extra help.

quiz.question: What did the narrator study years later, as an adult?
options: Medicine
A certificate in accounting
Art history
Engineering
quiz.explanation: She went back to studying for a certificate in accounting years later.

quiz.question: What is the narrator's final lesson about a good teacher?
options: A good teacher only teaches facts
A good teacher shows you learning is still possible no matter how late it starts
A good teacher should never be thanked
A good teacher makes students feel small
quiz.explanation: She concludes a good teacher shows you that learning is still possible, no matter how late it starts.
